text: Henry De La Warr Flood (September 2, 1865 – December 8, 1921) was a U.S. Representative from the Commonwealth of Virginia, brother of U.S. Representative Joel West Flood, and uncle of U.S. Senator Harry Flood Byrd. He was born in "Eldon," Appomattox County, Virginia, to Joel Walker Flood (1839–1916), a former Virginia state senator and Confederate States Army major, and his first wife, Ella Faulkner (1844–1885). He had an elder sister, Eleanor Bolling Flood Byrd (1864–1957), and a younger half-brother, Joel West Flood (1894–1964). Flood attended public schools in Appomattox and Richmond, Virginia, earning his undergraduate degree from Washington and Lee University and his law degree from the University of Virginia. He was admitted to the bar in 1886 and began practicing law in Appomattox. He served as Commonwealth's Attorney for Appomattox County in 1891, 1895, and 1899, and was elected as a delegate to the Virginia House of Delegates from 1887 to 1891. He then served in the Senate of Virginia from 1891 to 1903 and was a delegate to the Virginia Constitutional Convention of 1901. He ran unsuccessfully for the Fifty-fifth Congress. Flood was elected as a Democrat to the Fifty-seventh and ten succeeding Congresses, serving from March 4, 1901, until his death on December 8, 1921. In his first term, he proposed the creation of what later became Shenandoah National Park, an initiative realized decades later through the efforts of his nephew Harry F. Byrd, who became a U.S. Senator in 1933. He chaired the Committee on Foreign Affairs during the Sixty-second through Sixty-fifth Congresses and the Committee on Territories during the Sixty-second Congress. In 1911, he introduced the Flood amendment to the enabling act for New Mexico statehood, which allowed a simple majority to ratify amendments to the New Mexico Constitution. In 1917, he authored the resolutions that declared a state of war between the United States and Germany and Austria-Hungary, helping bring the U.S. into World War I. Henry Flood died in Washington, D.C., on December 8, 1921, and was interred in a mausoleum on the courthouse green in Appomattox, Virginia, within the Appomattox Historic District.
